doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

title: Rehearsing Rebirth of the Cool and musical conversation
summary: Mulligan led the Rebirth of the Cool tentet decisively, and small groups interact as a conversation.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: respect from the musicians that they would really, really buckle down when they were doing the rehearsals to show the respect. Sometimes not. Sometimes you would run into problems. But a guy like Gerry, that was never a problem. A guy like Marty Paich was never a problem, because they’re going to get up there, and Gerry didn’t care who it was. When we did those “Rebirth of the Cool” things we did a rehearsal before one of the concerts, that would have been in L.A. at A&M. Herb Alpert would let us use A&M sometimes when we needed to do rehearsals for something and we didn’t want a bunch of people just kind of showing up and keeping us from getting things done. And you know it had Lee Konitz and Art Farmer and Brookmeyer. Was Brookmeyer in that? I think Brookmeyer was part — it was either Brookmeyer or Rob McConnell. And you know this was an all-star tentet. It didn’t matter that it was Lee Konitz. It might have been somebody we’ve never heard of. It didn’t matter that it was Art Farmer. Gerry was, you know, if Lee did something Gerry wanted different he would tell him. If Art Farmer did something Gerry wanted done differently he would tell him. So he was a great leader from that standpoint and at certain occasions it makes my job a thousand times easier. But I know, again, that statement is very accurate from that standpoint but also again I think we’re talking about the democratic approach meaning ;that there’s a certain amount of freedom within a jazz ensemble that you don’t get otherwise, and those freedoms and how — because again with Gerry and Chet, and Gerry and the rhythm section from the original quartet, decisions, musical decisions as they were playing was made by them listening to each other and playing off of each other. I mean those things weren’t, even the beginnings — even the endings of things that sounded preconceived weren’t. These were guys who were very much aligned musically that were listening and playing off of each other, and of course in a small group setting, that’s the most enjoyable thing, when the musicians are truly having a musical conversation among themselves, and when the piano player plays a certain harmony to something the trumpet player, the saxophone hears it and goes that direction and so on and so forth. That’s the type of thing when I’m listening to things that I love to hear is when you really hear that interaction, so —
